Q: When to call QStyledItemDelegate.initStyleOption() on the QStyleOptionViewItem? A:

The QStyleOptionViewItem received by the delegate only contains a generically configured set of options, with all standard aspects set for the view, and very few others set specifically for the given index.

What initStyleOption() does is to read the data() specific to the given index, and properly "configure" the option based on it. This is necessary in order for calls of QStyledItemDelegate to be always consistent, and then use QStyle functions to properly do what necessary, such as return a proper size for the item based on its contents (which is also important for autoresizing of rows and columns), paint all items consistently, set the editor or update its geometry.

This is mostly done in order to get a single object, already configured as Qt would use it, which is easier to access and manage from any function that needs such information.

The view normally calls its viewOptions() and, depending on the function, eventually updates that option before "feeding" the delegate.

"Common" standard options are: view state (focus/active/etc.), decoration (size, position, alignment), display alignment, text elision and wrapping, view locale.
Options set by the view for the given index: the rect, some state flags (eg: if the index is hovered, or has focus), some of the features (eg: the alternate row).

In fact, the option you get in paint() is just slightly initialized: you only get some aspects set about the state or the features, but you're missing other ones, or you're getting them only generically set.

Specifically, the following aspects belonging to an index are not set for the option: the text (DisplayRole), the font (FontRole), the display alignment (TextAlignmentRole), the background (BackgroundRole) and foreground (ForegroundRole) colors or brushes, the check state (CheckStateRole), the decoration (DecorationRole, including its possible size when using a QPixmap or QImage) and all features related to aspects above (if the item contains text, a decoration, a check indicator).

All those aspects are automatically set by initStyleOption(), but can be obviously accessed in a function override by calling data() with the related roles, so, what's the point of that?

As long as your delegate does everything and correctly on its own, there's little point indeed. For instance, if you know for sure that your delegate will never show a checkstate or there's no custom background or icon set for different item, there's no point in calling initStyleOption() for something that you won't need.

But, in most cases, you want your custom delegate to still follow the default behavior (looking and behaving as more natively as possible), and only change the aspects you need.
That can only be done through calls to the functions of the view's QStyle, and those functions expect the related option to be properly filled, which is not the case of the option object received by related functions (such as paint() and sizeHint()), as that object has not been "finalized" for the index yet.

Another important aspect to consider is that the style option object is almost always reused within the same "main function call" of a view.
For instance, within the paintEvent() of a view, the delegate(s) will always receive the same QStyleOptionViewItem object, without checking if the delegate has changed its properties, so you should either never change those properties, or you should always create a copy of the object before altering and using it, otherwise you may end up with inconsistent behavior, because the next calls to the delegate's paint() will inherit those changes even if they're not consistent with the new index.

Q: How do you manage schema upgrades to a production database? A:

There are many libraries that automate the best practices of doing this.

I wrote a guide about it here: https://dev.to/tanin47/managing-the-database-schema-changes-for-your-app-14dn

To summarize the important points:

  • Check the database schema change scripts into git

  • A script contains the "up" migration (forward) and the "down" migration (revert)

  • Use a library to run those scripts automatically. In prod, we never run the down migration; it would simply fail. In dev, we run the down migration in order to get everyone's machine to be in sync.

    • The guide goes into the details and scenarios about this.

I've made a simple library for automating the database schema changes here: JMigrate https://github.com/tanin47/jmigrate or you can check out other alternatives like Flyway, Liquidbase, and MyBatis. They all work in a similar manner.

Q: Permission denied (publickey). Couldn't read packet: Connection reset by peer A:

Make sure the folder you're connecting to is owned by root and no other user/group has write priveleges:

sudo chown root:root /home/ftpuser/
sudo chmod 755 /home/ftpuser/

You can debug connection errors by using

sftp -vvv ftpuser@12.34.56.78
